title: Inquest cites gender issues, video glitch
article: A coroner's inquest jury made two recommendations this week after hearing about the circumstances surrounding the February death of Susan Maleska following her arrest on drug charges.

First, in "planned situations" such as drug raids, the jury recommended that efforts be made to "address gender issues," so that women prisoners can be more thoroughly searched. Second, they recommended the OPP review its "policies, procedures and protocols" to ensure that video equipment is recording when it should be.

Maleska, 44, died in Kingston General Hospital at 4:47 a.m. on Feb. 24 from a massive cocaine overdose. The jury found that her death was accidental, following her attempt to conceal an unknown quantity of cocaine by swallowing a plastic bag containing the drug.

Pathologist Dr. David Hurlbut, who performed Maleska's autopsy about nine hours after she died, testified that he found the plastic bag in the lower part of her esophagus. Hurlbut said the bag was later found to have contained cocaine. Blood samples sent to the centre also discovered lethal levels of cocaine and its metabolite, benzoylecgonine in Maleska's system.
Additionally, Hurlbut told the inquest his examination revealed that she had "a perforated nasal septum," consistent with "the chronic snorting of cocaine."

Hurlbut was also questioned by Coroner Dr. Benoit Bechard about the condition of Maleska's tongue. Mark Powell, the primary care paramedic who first began treated her in the cells area of the South Frontenac OPP detachment, told the jury that he'd observed a small amount of bright red blood around her mouth. Powell testified that it's not unusual for a patient to bite their tongue or the inside of their cheek during a seizure, such as Maleska had in the cells. But he didn't observe any injury. Dr. Hurlbut told jurors he found small lacerations at the front of Maleska's tongue during her autopsy that "would correlate with seizure activity."

The inquest heard testimony from the drug unit detective who arrested Maleska at her partner's Rutledge Road farmhouse around 1:33 a.m. that day, and the OPP officer who drove her to the detachment in Hartington an hour later. Both Det. Const. Craig Smith and OPP Const. Peter Robb said they detected no sign that she was in any distress.

Smith also testified that he had Maleska turn out her pockets and checked her socks for the presence of drugs or other objects before she was driven to the detachment. There were no female officers involved in the drug raid, however, and no female officers on duty that night at the detachment, who could have checked inside her bra or the waistband of her underwear.

The inquest wasn't able to judge Maleska's demeanour that night for themselves because her booking procedure wasn't videotaped. Robb told them he followed protocol by pushing the button to begin recording as soon as he arrived with Maleska. But the tape, as it turned out, needed changing and the alarm signal on the system couldn't be heard in the detachment garage.
